title: Intake limits for a healthy adult eating a solid food like bread: gastric capacity, eating rate, entry timing, eating MET, eligibility (task 5561, LN-2 {R-INTAKE})
source: Studies and consensus pages listed in sources.json under IL-* keys. Abstracts and page text read through fetch tools; several publisher pages (AJR, RSC, ScienceDirect, PubMed) returned HTTP 403 or a cookie wall, so where a figure is relayed from search-result text of a page not opened the Note column says so. A null Value, Low and High means no opened page gave the figure.
rows: Total gastric volume (contents) at maximum satiation after a mixed solid meal, by MRI

10 healthy adults (4 women), age 22 +/- 3, BMI 23 +/- 1; mixed solid meal (46% carbohydrate, 32% fat, 22% protein by energy) eaten at 100 kcal per 5 min until maximum satiation (rating 5 of 5); 300 mL water preload 10 min before; 1.5 T MRI

Mean +/- SD 657 +/- 186; proximal 110 +/- 40, distal 546 +/- 173 (Gastroenterology abstract). The volume of what is in the stomach (meal, secretion, any air, and the preload not yet emptied), not the volume of the meal. The page names neither the foods nor the mass of the solid meal.
Energy eaten before maximum satiation, mixed solid meal
10 healthy adults (4 women), age 22 +/- 3, BMI 23 +/- 1; same protocol as the gastric-volume row
Mean +/- SD 783 +/- 244 (liquid meal 630 +/- 353, p < 0.01 for the difference). Energy, not mass: converting to kg of bread needs the prepared bread's energy density from LN-1.
Time to maximum satiation, solid meal eaten at the imposed rate
10 healthy adults (4 women), age 22 +/- 3, BMI 23 +/- 1; intake held at 100 kcal per 5 min
Mean +/- SD 44 +/- 14 (liquid 31 +/- 17). The rate was set by the protocol, so this is not a free eating duration.
Intake rate imposed by the satiation protocol
10 healthy adults (4 women), age 22 +/- 3, BMI 23 +/- 1; 100 kcal every 5 minutes
Arithmetic on the stated protocol (100 kcal per 5 min). A protocol setting, never used as a natural eating rate.
Total gastric volume at maximum satiation after a liquid meal, by MRI
10 healthy adults (4 women), age 22 +/- 3, BMI 23 +/- 1; liquid meal of similar composition, same rate and protocol
Total gastric volume after the 300 mL water preload, solid-meal day, by MRI
10 healthy adults (4 women), age 22 +/- 3, BMI 23 +/- 1; 10 min after 300 mL water, before the meal

Mean +/- SD 271 +/- 59 (liquid-meal day 309 +/- 55). The Dig Liver Dis abstract also gives 554 +/- 203 mL at maximum satiation as a change from baseline, a different reference than the 657 mL of the Gastroenterology abstract; the two are kept apart.
Maximum tolerated intragastric balloon volume, normal-weight adults
11 normal-weight subjects (16 extremely obese in the same study); balloon in the stomach, water; maximal tolerable distension
Mean +/- 67 (SD or SE not stated). Measures how far a balloon distends a stomach to intolerance, not what a meal occupies. Satiety-like sensation at 541 +/- 44 mL.
Maximum tolerated intragastric balloon volume, extremely obese adults
Mean +/- 70 (SD or SE not stated); recorded as an evidence-supported effect of body composition on balloon capacity, not as a parameter.
Gastric capacity by balloon at discomfort rating 10, lean adults
Lean subjects (number not stated on the page for this part; 4 lean in the companion balloon-and-lunch part); balloon filled at 100 mL/min with 30 s pauses
Mean +/- 185 (SE). Capacity correlated with the balloon volume that halved a liquid lunch (r = 0.66, p < 0.05), not with spontaneous intake (r = 0.44, not significant).
Gastric capacity by balloon at discomfort rating 10, obese adults
Change in gastric capacity (maximum tolerated balloon volume) after 4 weeks on 600 kcal/day
14 obese adults (11 women) who lost 9.1 kg; 9 controls with no significant change
Percentage only: the abstract gives no baseline mL. A within-person change from body state; an obese population, so not applied to the healthy adult.
Maximum satiety volume, slow nutrient drinking test (15 mL/min)
18 healthy men aged 25 to 44; Ensure-H through a straw at 15 mL/min after a fast of more than 6 h; stopped at satiation score 5 or 1500 mL
Mean 731 (the paper's +/- 72 is not labelled SD or SE); Low and High are the range, High being the 1500 mL stop. No median. A liquid, not a solid meal.
Peak postprandial gastric (balloon) volume after drinking, peak accommodation
Same 18 men; barostat balloon on a separate day (up to 4 weeks later)
Mean +/- 27 (SD or SE not labelled). Preprandial balloon volume 172 +/- 15 mL.
Maximum tolerated volume of a nutrient drink in healthy controls
20 healthy controls, 20 functional dyspepsia patients, UltraMilk 0.6 kcal/mL, matched by age, sex and BMI

Value null: the opened journal page gives the diagnostic cut-off (950 mL or less; sensitivity 95%, specificity 100%) but not the controls' median or range, and the drinking rate. A search summary quoted a control median of 1375 mL (1000 to 1900); that text is not on the page opened and is not used.
Postprandial gastric volume change in excess of the ingested meal volume, by MRI
20 healthy volunteers, nutrient meal; MRI, SPECT for comparison

Mean +/- 12 (SEM). The excess was mainly air, 61 +/- 5 mL, the same whether the nutrient was taken in 30 or 150 mL aliquots (10 volunteers). What a volume cap must allow for beyond the food's own volume.
Air in the postprandial stomach beyond the ingested volume, by MRI
Mean +/- 5 (SEM). Liquid or nutrient meal, not a bread meal: whether chewed solid food carries more or less air is not in the abstract.
MRI gastric content volume 15 min after a 400 mL liquid meal
10 healthy volunteers (5 men, mean age 22); 200 mL Fortisip plus 200 mL water at 100 mL/min

Mean (SD 58). After subtracting secretion the meal-only volume was 338 (SD 50) mL; secretion 64 (SD 51) mL at 15 min and 110 (SD 40) mL at 75 min. Shows a measured stomach volume is the meal plus secretion.
Amount eaten by a competitive eater and a control in a speed-eating test
One world-class competitive eater and one control; fluoroscopy; single case

Value null: the abstract opened (Europe PMC) has no quantities and the AJR page returned HTTP 403, a second page (PubMed) needed cookies. Search-result text of secondary pages quoted 36 hot dogs in 10 minutes for the eater against 7 for the control, and water loading of 4.5 L against under 2 L; none of that was opened, so it is not a Value. One person, not a population.
Eating rate of plain bread slices

89 healthy normal-weight adults aged 18 to 30 (69 women), lunchtime sessions in sensory booths; foods eaten 'without stops between bites or sips', time by button press, sessions capped at 2 min; the group is 23 foods in the hard-and-dry plain-bread-slice class
Table value '9 (2-13)'; the table does not say whether 9 is a mean or median or whether 2 to 13 is a range across foods or across people. Eating time only, not time to finish a meal.
Eating rate of the reference whole-wheat bread, 35 g (one slice)
89 healthy normal-weight adults aged 18 to 30 (69 women), lunchtime sessions in sensory booths; reference food, first and third sessions
10 +/- 4.2 at the first session and 10 +/- 4.3 at the third (SD between people). Bread was the calibration reference for the other foods.
Eating rate of an ad libitum breakfast of sandwich slices with toppings
37 adults (11 men), age 24 +/- 7, BMI 23 +/- 3; three ad libitum breakfasts; bread plus topping (jam, syrup, cream cheese or egg salad) eaten together; total grams over total consumption time

Mean (SD 7.5); small buns 23.4 (7.5), large buns 24.3 (8.6). Relayed: the ScienceDirect page returned HTTP 403 and these numbers come from search-result text of the abstract, which the Europe PMC record does not carry. Includes the toppings' mass, so it is a meal rate, not a bread rate.
How much slower the slowest bread (wholemeal slice) is eaten than the fastest (soft white bun)
36 healthy adults, 25 +/- 6 y, BMI 22 +/- 2; nine bread types in a randomised crossover; video coding
P < 0.001; explained by smaller bites and more chews. Response-surface models predict eating rate from physical properties (R2 = 0.91) or sensory texture (R2 = 0.89).
Eating rate of each of nine bread types

Value null: the Europe PMC and WUR records give no g/min; the RSC article, its PDF and supplement returned HTTP 403 or 404 and the WUR PDF copies could not be read as text. A search summary showed '62 +/- 3' and '85 +/- 2' beside soft white bun and croissant without units; not used.
Rate implied by oral exposure time for 50 g portions of 35 savoury foods (not bread)
15 adults, 50 g of each food, video coded

Low and High are my arithmetic: 50 g over the reported 350 s (tortilla chips) and 27 s (canned tomatoes), level 5. The abstract names eating rate and bite size as measured but gives no numbers for them. Oral exposure time is not total eating time.
Within-person consistency of eating rate across meals (intraclass correlation)
146 adults (117 men) from four studies, the same or similar test meal on four non-consecutive days
The abstract says correlations were 'above 0.76' without a per-measure value. Faster eaters took larger bites (beta >= 0.39) and ate more energy. Between-person spread is not given in the abstract.
Time allowed to eat the standard test meal

Gastric emptying scintigraphy consensus (egg-white sandwich meal, about 255 kcal: 120 g egg white, two slices of white bread, jam, 120 mL water); at least 50% of each component eaten for the test to count
A protocol limit that clinics apply, not a measured intake rate. The meal contains bread.
Time zero of the gastric emptying curve relative to the end of the meal
Gastric emptying scintigraphy consensus, healthy and patient use; first image set 'immediately after meal ingestion', later images at 1, 2 and 4 h after ingestion

Percent-remaining is expressed against the first image, which is taken at the end of the meal. This is the protocol's convention: the meal itself takes up to 10 min and no emptying during those minutes is modelled or measured.
A source stating a meal enters the stomach at one instant for emptying models
Searched: Abell 2008 consensus, Tougas 2000 abstract, the R package gastempt page, Siegel 1988 and Elashoff 1982 through search summaries

Value null: no opened page says a meal enters at one instant. The consensus starts curves at the end of ingestion. The Tougas abstract does not say when imaging starts; the gastempt page does not define t = 0; Siegel 1988 and Elashoff 1982 were not opened.
2024 Adult Compendium of Physical Activities, ages 19 to 59; 1 MET = 3.5 mL/kg/min

The page marks estimated values in red and the text copy lost the colour, so whether 13030 is measured or estimated is not known from this page. Of 1,114 activities 202 are estimated. The 2011 compendium supplement was fetched but is a binary PDF the tool could not read, so the 2011 row is unconfirmed.
MET of talking and eating or eating only, standing (code 13035)
2024 Adult Compendium of Physical Activities, ages 19 to 59
Same provenance caveat as 13030. The description joins talking with eating, so it is not an eating-only cost.
Oral feeding of a patient with a reduced level of consciousness
ACCP evidence-based guideline (Grade B), patients with oral-pharyngeal dysphagia risk

Statement, no number: patients with a reduced level of consciousness 'should not be fed orally until the level of consciousness has improved'. A clinical recommendation about aspiration risk, not a measured limit on swallowing.
Decreased level of consciousness as an aspiration risk factor
Review of the literature on aspiration in tube-fed and other patients

Statement, no number: decreased level of consciousness is 'a major risk factor for aspiration'; the abstract carries no effect size and the review notes small samples and equivocal definitions of aspiration.
